## R-656. A failure a person can repair is recorded permanent, so since R-390 it needs a fresh job

**Found by** R-390's build, 2026-09-22, driving the eleven tests that re-armed
through `jobs.retry` after a fake failure.

`Cause.retryable` defaults to false, and `jobs.retry` now refuses a closed job
whose cause carries false. Two workers record a failure a person can put right
as permanent by that default. Mastering records `source-missing` and
`encoder-missing` with the flag unset, so a recording placed after the failure,
or an encoder installed after it, does not reopen the job. Acquisition records
`adapter-broken` permanent on purpose, R-348, because a defect retried for ever
is worse, and the engine's item boundary records any bare exception as
`internal-error`, permanent, on the same judgement. Backup's transfer exit was
the third and is fixed in the same unit: a dropped connection mid mirror is
retryable now.

**Measured cost.** Two tests, `tests/test_master_cli.py` and
`tests/test_acquire_workers.py`, model the repair then resume path and now
assert the refusal. A person who repairs the cause queues the work again the
way it was queued the first time, which the refusal's steps say; the items
that succeeded are durable and the mastering test shows the fresh job
completing. Unmeasured live.

**Closes when:** a failure the person can repair without changing the program
is marked retryable at its raise site, mastering's two are the candidates, or
the resume verb gains an explicit re-arm the person asks for over a permanent
verdict, or the two are left permanent with the reason written beside them.

**Not on the board bar.** The refusal names the act, the work can be queued
again, and nothing is lost or reported falsely.

## R-658. Eleven `monkeypatch.undo()` calls restore the real machine mid test, and nothing guards a plain battery run

**Found:** by R-343's session, 2026-09-22, reading the mechanism behind the
2026-09-20 overwrite.

`tests/conftest.py` isolates HOME, the XDG variables, both Cratekit overrides,
the keychain and the library root with `monkeypatch`, which is one
function scoped instance shared by the autouse fixtures and the test body. An
`undo()` in the body reverts all of it, and from that line the test runs on the
real machine. Eleven calls: `tests/test_adoption.py` five,
`tests/test_reserved_causes.py` two, `tests/test_uncredited_tombstone.py`,
`tests/test_outbound_workers.py`, `tests/test_restore.py` and
`tests/intake/test_repair_apply.py` one each. The trap is already in
`docs/solutions/` and has no guard.

**Measured cost.** On the clean tree, none: a full suite run left the real state
directory byte for byte unchanged, 9971 tests. On a mutated tree, one real
configuration on 2026-09-20. The mutation driver's children are now sandboxed
by R-343's fix. A plain `pytest` run is not: its process starts with the real
values, and an `undo()` in it restores them.

**Why not fixed here.** Scope was held to the driver on 2026-09-22, Phillip's
call, because the driver is the only thing that runs a mutated tree. Each of
the eleven needs its own reasoning about what it meant to undo, and a
session scoped tripwire in the conftest was considered and declined.

**Closes when:** every `monkeypatch.undo()` in `tests/` is replaced by a scoped
patch, or the conftest fingerprints the real installation state at session
start and fails the session if it changed, and a test drives an undo followed
by a write and shows it land in the temp root.

**On the board bar under (a).** Files were damaged, and demonstrably. Issue filed after the merge that carries this entry.

**Closed 2026-09-23 on `relay/191`, on its first condition and with the guard
the second one lacked.** Neither route the brief offered. The tripwire was
declined again because it detects the write after it happens, and the scoped
route alone fixes eleven instances and not the class. So the six root conftest
fixtures that isolate the machine (state roots, keychain, provider client,
recognition transport, mix fetcher, library root and mount check) each hold
their own `pytest.MonkeyPatch.context()` and request no `monkeypatch`. That
keeps them set up before the body's instance and torn down after it, so a body
`undo()` reverts the body's patches and nothing of theirs. All eleven sites are
now scoped patches around the one call each was for. Two of them were leaning
on the wider revert: the restore retry lost its own "nothing is running" stub,
and repair apply rebuilt the library root and `config.load` by hand after
throwing them away. The built in review found the class one file over, about
two dozen module level autouse guards still on the shared instance, so a new
test walks `tests/` and refuses any `monkeypatch.undo()`, exempting only the
guard file by exact path. `tests/test_isolation_survives_undo.py` undoes a body
patch, then resolves the platformdirs and product config and state paths, the
keychain, the library root and the refusals. It asserts each is inside the
test's temp root before writing, so the four undo tests fail against `main`'s
conftest without writing. Tables `docs/mutation/r658-a.md` to `r658-d.md`, read
in `r658-notes.md`: 22 rows, 20 killed, S4's zero paired with a composite that
kills, and one maintainer zero. The real state directory was fingerprinted
before and after two full battery runs, 2446 entries, unchanged.

## R-660. The guard cannot tell a child's write from a concurrent one

**Found:** by the built in review of R-343's fix, 2026-09-22.

The comparison is against the batch's starting fingerprint. A `crate` run in
another terminal writes a run record into the same directory and stops the
batch exactly as a leak would, and the row that was running is named.

**Measured cost:** none observed; the message says which of the two it could
not tell. A stopped batch is a rerun, and the rerun is minutes.

**Why not fixed here.** Distinguishing them means the child reporting what it
wrote, which is the plugin's job and a larger change than a message.

**Closes when:** a concurrent writer is driven mid batch and the report names
it as concurrent rather than as the row, or the rule that nothing else uses the
directory during a batch is enforced by a lock the driver takes.

## R-661. A promoted row's full suite death can be the repository scan reading the driver's own sidecar

**Found:** by R-343's own first table, 2026-09-22. Four rows killed zero on
`tests/test_mutation_driver.py`, were promoted to the full suite, and were each
reported killed by exactly one test,
`tests/test_portability.py::test_the_repository_itself_is_clean`.

That test runs `scan.scan_tree` over the repository with identity checking on.
The driver writes its progress sidecar into `docs/mutation/` after the first
row, and anything in that sidecar the scan refuses fails the test on every full
suite run that follows. R-343's sidecar carried the guarded root under the home
directory, so it named the account. The null control did not die because it
runs before the sidecar exists, which is what let the artifact pass for a
measurement.

**Measured cost.** Read across every committed `docs/mutation/*.json`: 37
promoted rows report a death, and 11 of them are killed by the cleanliness test
alone, four in R-343's first table and seven in earlier ones, `u28-skills-independent`
among them. Each of those eleven is a zero row that the table records as
killed, which is the opposite of what a mutation table is for. R-343's four
were re-measured after the sidecar was made portable, see `docs/mutation/r343.md`;
the seven earlier ones were not re-run here.

**Why not fixed here.** Both fix rounds were spent, the second on making
R-343's own sidecar portable, which removes this unit's instance and not the
class. The class is that the driver's artifact is inside the tree the suite
scans.

**Closes when:** the driver classifies a promoted row whose only killer is the
cleanliness test as a zero and says so, or the sidecar is written outside the
tree during the run and moved into `docs/mutation/` at the end, and the seven
earlier rows are re-measured or their tables annotated.

**Not on the board bar.** Maintainer facing: nothing a person using the
shipped verbs pays for.

## R-662. A setup re-run cannot repair a spelled backup remote that disagrees with the destinations

**Found:** at the fifth attended sitting, 2026-09-23, rebuilding the
configuration R-343's leak destroyed.

The leaked fixture file spelled `remote = "remote"`. R-345's rule derives the
remote from the destinations only when the file does not spell one, and the
destinations given on the command line named `gdrive`, so setup refused under
`config-unusable` naming the disagreement, and its own fix line said
`crate setup`. No flag sets or clears `backup.remote`, so the re-run it
recommends reproduces the refusal. The sitting moved the fixture file out of the
state directory by hand, as sitting 1 did with the same class of debris.

**Measured cost.** One refused run and a hand move of the configuration file,
on a machine where the file was already known to be fixture data. On a machine
where a person had mistyped the remote, the same loop holds and the fix line
points back at itself.

**Why not fixed here.** A sitting's write to the wizard is a unit's work, and
the wizard's flag set was decided by R-345 a day earlier.

**Closes when:** setup takes `--backup-remote`, or derives the remote from the
destinations whenever the given destinations agree among themselves and the
recorded remote is not among rclone's, and the refusal's fix line names the
flag rather than the command that just refused.

**Not on the board bar.** Maintainer facing: a recovery path, nothing lost,
nothing false.

**Closed 2026-09-25 on `relay/211`, issue #211.** Setup takes
`--backup-remote`, an explicit answer that replaces a recorded remote. Without
it, `_replace_a_remote_rclone_lacks` replaces a spelled remote the
destinations disagree with, when the destinations agree among themselves,
rclone's configuration was READ, rclone has no remote by the spelled name,
and it does have the destinations' one, and a `setup.backup.remote` note says
so. That last condition is narrower than the closing line above, on purpose:
an empty dump lacks every name, and there a right remote beside mistyped
destinations would be swapped for the typo. Where rclone knows the spelled
remote, or is missing, or cannot be read, R-345's rule stands and validation
refuses. That refusal carries no `run-setup` token when the disagreement is
its only problem, so the fix line is the first step, "re-run crate setup with
--backup-remote <name>", naming the destinations' remote and the other way
out. Beside other problems the token stays and the flag leads the steps. The
validator's own problem text names the flag too, so a refusal from any verb
that loads the file carries it. The agreement rule is one public function,
`config.backup_remote_disagreement`, read by the validator, the repair and
the refusal. Sitting 5's producer, a file spelling `remote` and destinations
naming `gdrive`, is driven through the dispatcher both ways
(`tests/test_doctor.py`). Mutation table in `docs/mutation/r662-a.md`,
`r662-b.md` and `r662-notes.md`, 22 rows, one maintainer facing zero. Filed
R-721 from the review.

## R-663. Setup accepts a zero byte database path and reports it as a missing table on the copy

**Found:** at the fifth attended sitting, 2026-09-23.

`PIONEER/rekordbox/master.db` on the library volume is a zero byte file dated
2026-05-21, one directory over from the live `PIONEER/Master/master.db`. Given
as `--db-path`, setup recorded it, copied it, and the canary read failed with
`no such table: agentRegistry` on the copy, twice, once for the canary and once
for the prefix rule offer, each with the full SQL statement. `db_containment`
passed, since the file sits under the root. Nothing said the file was empty.

**Measured cost.** One setup run and the pin and prefix rule not recorded
until the path was corrected. The wrong path came from a `find` that returned
both files and an author who took the first one. A configuration recorded
against that path reads as a library with no tables, and every verb that opens
a copy fails the same way with the same statement.

**Why not fixed here.** A sitting fix on setup's path validation belongs in a
session with the canary's tests.

**Closes when:** setup refuses a database path whose file is empty, or whose
copy has none of the tables the canary reads, under a cause that names the
size and the path rather than the table, and doctor reports the same.

**Not on the board bar.** Maintainer facing: the wrong path was the author's,
and the product refused rather than proceeding.

**Closed 2026-09-25 on `relay/210`, issue #210.** `rb_writer.read_only_copy`
refuses a copy that is empty BEFORE the open, and a copy whose canary read
failed and whose own schema lists neither `agentRegistry` nor `djmdContent`,
both under a new slug, `library-database-not-rekordbox`, at the
`LIBRARY_UNAVAILABLE` code beside `library-database-missing`. The message
names the configured path and the copy's size, "is empty, 0 bytes" or "is N
bytes and holds none of the tables a rekordbox library keeps", never the
table, and the remedy is `run-setup` with a step naming `--db-path` and the
one master.db that is not empty. A copy holding one of the two tables stays
`canary-read-failed`, since that is drift, and so does a file whose tables
could not be listed, and a refusal raised before the canary keeps its own
slug. Setup's `_refuse_a_database_that_is_not_one` takes the copy after the
answers validate and before the pin, the drive rule and the save, and stops
on that one slug, so nothing is recorded; a missing file, a running
rekordbox, and any other refusal are left to the notes and doctor as before.
Doctor's `library.paths_resolved` carries the same cause and remedy through.
The review's two declined findings, kept here so they are not re-raised:
setup now copies the database once more per run, which was kept rather than
threading one copy through the drive rule, whose early return on a recorded
map would skip the check; and the refusal lands after every question rather
than at the path question, because the copy is opened under the pins the
whole answer set describes. Filed R-719 and R-720.

## R-664. The index takes the title tag with its head on, so no processed file resolves owned and every heart is offered or missing

**Found:** at the sixth attended sitting, 2026-09-23, on the first live `crate
intake playlist favorites`.

The job resolved the account's 206 listed hearts against the library: **0 owned,
61 offered, 145 missing.** Sitting 4's favourites sweep had matched 59 of those
same hearts to library rows by ISRC; the intake worker resolved 37 of the 59 as
missing and 22 as offered. `match._read_from_disk` takes a file's title from its
tag first, verbatim, and strips heads only from the filename stem. In this
library the Title tag carries the same `KEY - BPM - ` head the filename does,
`06A - 126 - Dr. Beat` for a file the provider spells `Dr. Beat`, the live
system's convention that R-168 records. So the recording token of every
processed file holds the head, an exact match is impossible, and the approximate
pass either offers the file as `title-approximate` or, when the head outweighs a
short title, scores it under the floor of 82 and reports missing.

**Measured on the tree, 2026-09-23.** 9767 of 9868 files under the music folder
index with a head in their title. The 206 frozen rows of job
`2026-09-23T17:21:30Z-0dbf`, resolved against the same volume with a reader that
passes the tag title through `naming.strip_heads` and nothing else changed: **96
owned, 27 offered, 83 missing**, against the shipped reader's 0, 61 and 145 on
the same rows in the same process. Of sitting 4's 59, 37 matched outright, 8
were offered and 14 stayed missing, those 14 being rows whose artist tag lists
every credited artist where the provider names one, a second and narrower gap
that the ISRC both sides carry would close, unmeasured beyond that count.

**Measured cost, and it is the whole acquisition workflow.** `crate intake
missing --job` writes the missing rows to the list `acquire download` reads, so
the next step of A5 line 1 would have listed at least 96 owned tracks, and the
download and the landing after it would have put 96 duplicates into the library
and the collection. Every playlist intake, the inbound check of `crate sync
all`, `intake set` and `match run` read the same index and say missing over the
same files. The sitting stopped at the listing, with job `0dbf` succeeded and
its 61 review items unanswered.

**Why not fixed here.** The reader is the one every caller of the index shares,
and R-71 and R-168 sit on the same seam. A unit's work, not a sitting's.

**Closes when:** a file whose title tag carries a head indexes under the head
stripped title, driven against a tag spelled `06A - 126 - Dr. Beat` and a
provider row spelling `Dr. Beat`, and the 206 frozen rows of job `0dbf`
re-resolved on the live library report none of sitting 4's 59 missing for the
head alone.

**On the board bar, (b) and (a):** the product says missing over 96 tracks the
library holds, and the list it writes from that has `acquire download` put
duplicates into the library. Issue owed after this commit.

**Closed 2026-09-23 on its first condition, by the unit for issue #192.**
`match._read_from_disk` passes the title tag through `naming.strip_heads`
under the same template the stem strips under, before the pair rule, so a tag
of `06A - 126 - Dr. Beat` indexes as `Dr. Beat` and a provider row spelling
`Dr. Beat` resolves matched, driven against a real container in
`tests/test_match_states.py` and through `intake playlist` and `intake missing
--job` in `tests/test_intake_missing.py`, where a file held under a headed tag
is owned and nothing is written. A tag that is only a head strips to empty and
falls to the filename, the branch an absent tag takes. The head inside the tag
carries the key when the stem has none, below the stem's head and above the
`initialkey` tag, which reverses the unit's first draft: the review drove a
file that indexed with no key until a rename padded the same head into its
filename, so one file gave two answers, and `write/naming_cli.py` already read
the head off either surface. A release genuinely ending in a code and a number
loses that tail on the tag as it always has on the stem, and a test names it.
**The second condition, the 206 frozen rows of job `0dbf` re-resolved on the
live library with none of sitting 4's 59 missing for the head alone, is the
next sitting's measurement**, attended, over a fresh listing, as the brief and
`docs/cutover.md` say. The four other readers that take the title tag
verbatim are R-665.

**Closed 2026-09-23 on its second condition, at the seventh attended
sitting.** Job `2026-09-23T18:12:52Z-7caa`, the same 206 rows as `0dbf` over a
fresh listing, resolved 96 owned, 29 offered and 81 missing, against the
reader's 0, 61 and 145 and the measured 96, 27 and 83. Of sitting 4's 59, 37
owned, 9 offered and 13 missing, and every one of the 22 reads its head off

## R-665. The tagging searchers ask the catalogue for the headed title, so a processed file's genre search is a query nobody released

**Found by** the built in review of the unit for issue #192, 2026-09-23,
hunting the shape R-664 fixed one file over.

`tagging/tag.py:tag_one` and `tagging/retag.py` read the title tag verbatim
and hand it to the searcher as the title, `hit = searcher(artist, title)`.
`intake/ingest.py` strips a leading head only, through `strip_head`, and
`intake/normalize.from_audio_file` takes the tag verbatim into a `Wanted` that
neither of its two callers resolves against the index, so those two carry no
cost today and are named so the next reader of this seam does not re-derive
that. The two searchers do carry one.

**Driven, 2026-09-23.** `tag_one` over a real container tagged
`06A - 126 - Dr. Beat` by `Felixcw` asked its searcher for
`('Felixcw', '06A - 126 - Dr. Beat')`. One candidate was driven and it
produces the input. `retag` was read, not driven, and reads the same two tags
the same way three lines before its own search.

**Measured cost, and where it lands.** `tag folder` runs over freshly
downloaded files before analysis writes a head, so on the shipped pipeline the
title it searches is plain and the cost is not reached; that is stated from
the pipeline's order, not driven. `retag` runs over library files, 9767 of
9868 of which carry the head inside the tag, so a retag sweep searches the
catalogue for a headed title on nearly every file, gets no hit, and asks
rather than answers. The size of that miss rate against the real catalogue is
unmeasured.

**Why not fixed here.** The unit's seam is the index reader. The review's
proposed shape is one title reader on the tags or naming seam, taking the
template and stripping both ends, called from all five sites, and that is a
decision about a helper four modules share rather than a repair to one.

**Closes when:** every reader that compares a title tag with a provider
spelling strips the head under the library's template through one shared
call, and a retag over a headed real container asks its searcher for the plain
title.

**Not on the board bar.** A search that misses becomes a question in the
review queue, not a false answer, a lost file or a blocked verb, and the one
verb that reaches it is a sweep a person runs deliberately.

## R-666. The index reader opens every container three times, and the walk is the library

**Found by** the built in review of the unit for issue #192, 2026-09-23.
R-169's shape, on the index reader rather than the rename.

`match._read_from_disk` calls `tags.read_tag` for the artist, the title and
the `initialkey`, and each call opens and parses the container. The unit did
not add a read: the tag head is parsed off the title already read. It did not
remove one either. `index_library` walks the whole music folder, so every
playlist intake, the inbound check of `sync all`, `intake set` and `match run`
pay three parses per file over 9868 files.

**Measured cost.** Not measured in seconds, and the report says so. The shape
is roughly thirty thousand container opens per walk against about ten
thousand, on an external volume.

**Why not fixed here.** A one open reader is a change to the tags seam,
`read_tags(path, fields)` or a shape like `read_tag_values`, and the unit's
seam is the index.

**Closes when:** the reader opens each container once and the walk over a
fixture of a thousand files is timed against the current one.

**Not on the board bar.** Maintainer facing: slow, not wrong.

**Closed 2026-09-23 by the unit for issue #193, which needed it.** The brief
forbade a fourth open for the ISRC, so `tags.read_tags(path, fields)` opens a
container once and answers each field exactly as `read_tag` does, and
`read_tag` is now one field of it. `match._read_from_disk` reads its four
fields through one call, and a test counts the opens. Timed over a fixture of
a thousand real containers on the local disk, three walks each: one open
0.14 s, the three open reader it replaces 0.21 s, the four open shape 0.30 s.
The live volume, external, was walked once reading two fields for the
credited list measurement: 9868 files in 11.7 s. Not timed against the three
open reader on the volume.

## R-667. The match engine never consults the ISRC, and a processed file's artist tag lists every credited artist, so a quarter of the hearts the library holds read missing or offered

**Found:** at the seventh attended sitting, 2026-09-23, on the second live
`crate intake playlist favorites`, the first over the index that strips the
head from the title tag (R-664). R-664 named this gap as "second and
narrower" and put it at 14 rows, unmeasured beyond that count. Measured on the
tree it is 49 of 206, a quarter of the account's hearts.

**The mechanism.** `match._read_from_disk` takes the artist tag verbatim, and
in this library the artist tag lists every credited artist, `Malive, Tito
Azevedo, MRQZ`, where the provider row names the primary artist alone,
`Malive`. `recording_token` joins the folded artist and the folded title, so
the file's recording is `malive tito azevedo mrqz / burning` and the wanted one
is `malive / burning`, and an exact match is impossible however the title
reads. The approximate pass then either offers the file as `title-approximate`
or, when the credited list outweighs the title, scores it under the floor and
reports missing. Both sides carry the ISRC: R-355 made the file's tag readable
through `source.isrc_for`, and every report the intake worker writes carries
the provider row's, but `Owned` has no ISRC field and the index cannot be asked
by one. `BY_ISRC` in the same module is the acquisition candidate search on the
provider side, not a library lookup.

**Measured on the tree, 2026-09-23.** Job `2026-09-23T18:12:52Z-7caa`, the
same 206 rows as `0dbf`: 96 owned, 29 offered, 81 missing. The music folder
walked by ISRC tag, 9868 files, 1691 of them with no ISRC tag: **26 of the 81
missing rows and 23 of the 29 offered rows are held under the row's own
ISRC.** Of sitting 4's 59 hearts matched to rows by ISRC, 37 owned, 9 offered,
13 missing, and every one of the 22 reads its head off correctly and fails on
the artist alone, which is R-664's second condition, met. `intake missing
--job` wrote all 81 rows to the list, 26 of them held. Held rows include
`Nico Szabo, Aske Izan :: Paranoid` against the provider's `Nico Szabo`,
`Ferreck Dawn, Hayley May :: Deep Inside` against `Ferreck Dawn`, and
`Traumer, antraum, Anton :: Hyaku` against `antraum`, where the primary artist
is not even first in the list.

**Measured cost.** `acquire download` over the product's own list puts 26
duplicates into staging, and `intake land` after it would put them into the
library and the collection. The 23 offered rows are questions a person is
asked about files the library plainly holds, and an answer of no lists them
for download too (R-503). The sitting hand built a list of the 55 unheld rows
and downloaded those, so nothing duplicate reached staging.

**Why not fixed here.** The index is the seam every caller shares, R-71,
R-168 and R-664 sit on it, and an ISRC lookup changes the shape of `Owned`
and `LibraryIndex`. Two rules would close it and the unit chooses: an ISRC
lookup first, exact and cheap, which the 1691 files without an ISRC tag
cannot use; and a credited list rule, the provider's primary artist a member
of the file's list, for the rest. A unit's work, not a sitting's.

**Closes when:** a file whose artist tag lists several credited artists and
whose ISRC tag matches the provider row resolves owned, driven against a real
container tagged `Malive, Tito Azevedo, MRQZ` and `04A - 126 - Burning
(Extended Mix)` with ISRC `USNRS2644532` and a provider row spelling `Malive`
and `Burning (Extended Mix)` under the same ISRC; and the 206 rows of job
`7caa` re-resolved on the live library report none of the 49 held by ISRC as
missing or offered.

**On the board bar, (a) and (b):** the product says missing over 26 tracks the
library holds and its own list has `acquire download` put duplicates into the
library, and it asks 23 questions over files it holds. Issue owed after this
merge.

**Closed 2026-09-23 on its first condition, by the unit for issue #193.**
Two rules, in the order the entry proposed. `Owned` carries the file's ISRC
tag folded through `match.isrc_token`, `LibraryIndex.by_isrc` can be asked by
it, and `resolve_one` asks before any text rule: a file carrying the row's
ISRC whose folded title agrees is owned under a reason of its own,
`isrc-exact`, the key still checked over those files, driven against a real
container tagged `Malive, Tito Azevedo, MRQZ` and `04A - 126 - Burning
(Extended Mix)` with ISRC `USNRS2644532` and a provider row spelling `Malive`
and `Burning (Extended Mix)` under the same ISRC, in
`tests/test_match_states.py`, and through `intake playlist` then `intake
missing --job` in `tests/test_intake_missing.py`, where it is owned and
nothing is written. For the files with no ISRC tag, `LibraryIndex.held`
applies the credited list rule after the recording token: a file whose folded
title is the row's and whose comma separated artist tag credits the row's
primary artist as one whole member is the same recording, under
`credited-exact`, driven on the same container with its ISRC removed and on
`Traumer, antraum, Anton` against `antraum`. Whole names, never substrings.
A credited hit at another version is the version question it is. The built
in review at high raised eight findings and all were driven: an ISRC agrees
only with the folded title and a file carrying the ISRC under another title
is offered as a question with its path rather than called owned (R-674); an
ISRC settled row lists the files carrying it and no text copy; an ISRC
settles the version on the candidate too; the fold has one owner,
`match.fold_isrc` and `match.isrc_token`, called by the outbound source and
the missing verb; members are computed once per file. The reader takes its
four fields through one container open (R-666). The comma is the only joiner,
measured on the live volume (R-673). **The second condition, the 206 rows of
job `7caa` re-resolved on the live library with none of the 49 held by ISRC
missing or offered, is the next sitting of #178, attended.** This unit's walk
of the same folder counted 1588 files with no ISRC tag against the sitting's
1691, both read through `tags`, and the difference is recorded and not
explained: no mechanism is offered without a measurement showing it.

**CLOSED on its second condition 2026-09-23, sitting 8 of #178.** The 206
rows of job `7caa` re-resolved on the live library as job
`2026-09-23T22:34:35Z-c645` on the pipx install at `93e8f40`: **203 owned, 2
offered, 1 missing**, and all 49 rows held by ISRC at sitting 7 owned under
`isrc-exact`, none missing, none offered. By reason across the 206: 198
`isrc-exact`, 4 `credited-exact`, 1 `exact`, 1 `version-differs`, 1
`title-approximate`, 1 `not-in-library`. The 4 credited hits are files in a
processed folder with no ISRC tag, three Steve Reich movements and one
Breaking Beattz row, the rule's second half working live. The missing row is
the lossy only heart, refused by policy. Record in `docs/cutover.md`, sitting 8.

## R-668. The download verb's resume needs the list named again

**Found:** at the seventh attended sitting, 2026-09-23. `crate acquire
download --job <id>` refuses with argparse's "the following arguments are
required: list", though the help says the flag continues the acquisition
already queued and the queued job froze the list's absolute path. The resume
argv the product builds for itself carries the list, so nothing automated is
affected; a person continuing a job by hand types the path a second time.

**Closes when:** `--job` alone drives the queued job, reading the frozen list
path off the job, or the help says the list is required either way.

**Not on the board bar.** A wording and shape fix, no data at risk.

**Closed 2026-09-24 on `relay/208`, issue 208.** `--job` alone drives the
queued job. The `list` positional of `acquire download` is optional and its
help says to omit it with `--job`, which froze it. The resume never read the
list: the job carries the frozen path and every track. `download_argv` is now
`acquire download --job <id>`, so the respawned child and the "drive it with"
line R-678 prints both name the job alone. A list named beside `--job` is
checked against the frozen path, after the freeze's own absolutising and then
`preflight._names_one_path`. The same file still drives, so a saved command in
the old two argument form works. A different one is refused as
`intake-list-unusable`, before the sweep and the reconcile, because driving
the job would report the named list acquired when another was. A command
naming neither, and an empty `--job ""`, are refused at the head of the verb
before the configuration is read. The empty identifier used to fall through to
the queueing path and queue the list again. Tests in
`tests/test_acquire_workers.py` under the R-668 heading. The mutation table
`docs/mutation/r668-a` and `r668-b`, twelve rows, every one killed. The same
shape one file over is R-718.

## R-669. An acquired file is named for its provider identifier and no verb ever names it, so a landed batch is fifty four numbers

**Found:** at the seventh attended sitting, 2026-09-23, on the first `crate
name apply --root` over a folder `acquire download` had filled.

Two decisions, each recorded and each sound alone, meet in a hole. The
vendored adapter names the file it lands `{track_id}` on purpose, "naming is
U4's engine working from the declared template, and letting the downloader
choose a library name would put a second naming authority in the pipeline"
(`acquire/vendored.py`, `STAGING_TEMPLATE`). The naming verb, by R-168's
decision, pads the head it understands and leaves the body it does not:
`write/naming_cli.py:_spec_for` takes the stem through `strip_head` and never
composes a body from the artist and title tags. A freshly acquired file has
no head to pad, since the tempo has no tag field and the only source of one
is a filename head the file does not have, and its body is the identifier. So
the plan renders every name unchanged.

**Measured on the tree, 2026-09-23.** Fifty four files in download staging,
every one named `<id>.flac`, thirty nine with an `initialkey` tag: the plan
is `count 0, referenced 0, collides 0`, items empty, on both output forms.
The landing plan after it moves the same fifty four names into
`Music/<batch>/`. The tags are complete, artist, title, ISRC, genre on forty
and art on all, so rekordbox will show the track; the file on disk, on a
player browsing folders, on a USB, and in any listing outside rekordbox, is a
number.

**Measured cost, and it is for life.** U67 made `name apply` refuse a file
the collection references (R-407), which every landed file is once it is
imported. So the sequence the design names, `tag folder`, `name apply`,
`intake land`, the import, lands a file the product can never name
afterwards. The source system named at download, `Artist - Title`, and the
head was padded later by its pad stage.

**Why not fixed here.** The naming seam owns it and R-168 is the recorded
decision not to recompose a body. The narrower rule that does not reopen

## R-674. A file carrying the row's ISRC under another title is offered as a question, and whether the volume holds one is unmeasured

**Found by** the built in review of the unit for issue #193, 2026-09-23. The

that makes: a bootleg or edit ingested with the original's tags, or a tagger
that wrote one ISRC across a release, carries ISRC X under a different title,
the heart for X resolves owned to that file, its paths point at the wrong
recording, and the row is never acquired with nothing saying so.

**The conservative call, taken.** `resolve_one` settles a row by ISRC only
when the file's folded title agrees with the row's. A file carrying the ISRC
under a different title is offered as a `title-approximate` question with its
path, so a person decides, and it is never called owned on one tag. The
review drove the shape on a fixture, `tests/test_match_states.py`, the test
named for an ISRC hit whose title disagrees.

volume disagree on the folded title. Sitting 7's 22 rows from sitting 4's
sample read their heads off correctly and failed on the artist alone, so
those 22 agree; the other 27 were not read for it. If some disagree, the
next sitting sees them offered rather than owned, which is a question and
not a listing for download.

**The other option, recorded.** Trust the ISRC outright, as the brief's
wording "an exact ISRC hit is owned" reads. It costs a wrong owned over a
mis-tagged file, silent, against a question over a right one, visible. The
unit took the visible cost.

**Closes when:** the next sitting of #178 reports the 49 held rows by
reason, `isrc-exact`, `credited-exact` and offered, and any offered row
whose file carries the row's ISRC is decided one way or the other.

**Not on the board bar.** The product asks rather than answers, over a
population it cannot yet size, and the cost of the alternative is the one
board bar (b) names.

**CLOSED 2026-09-23, sitting 8 of #178, measured at zero.** The 49 rows held
by ISRC resolved 49 `isrc-exact`, 0 `credited-exact`, 0 offered, so every
held file agrees with its row on the folded title. Across the whole job, no

## R-675. R-500's dark row guard refused every live rename plan, because rekordbox records a streamed track as a slash path and a real library carries hundreds of tombstones under folders that are gone

**Found:** at the eighth attended sitting, 2026-09-23, on the first `crate
name apply --root` over download staging after R-669's unit, the first live
plan that would rename anything. The verb refused `collection-row-unmapped`,
582 rows, before the gate, and renamed nothing. Sitting 7's run of the same
verb over the same folder reached the gate, because its plan was empty and
`_plan_for` reads the collection only when something would be renamed, so the
guard had never once been consulted on the live library.

**The mechanism.** R-500's rule: a row no prefix rule resolves whose recorded
file is absent is DARK, and one dark row refuses the whole verb, since its only
key is a spelling nothing here carries and the file it names could be any
candidate under another spelling. Measured on a disposable copy of the live
database, 17341 rows, the 582 are 137 active rows recorded as
`/v4/catalog/tracks/<id>/`, which is how rekordbox 7 records a streamed Tidal
track, a form that starts with a slash and so reaches
`locations.resolve_recorded_path` as an absolute path rather than the colon
form the resolver excuses as `NOT_A_PATH`; 252 tombstones under a device
content tree, 184 tombstones under the old `Original_Tracks` folder in the home
directory, both gone; and 9 rows on the other account of this machine. The
guard's own docstring said a streaming pseudo-location contributes nothing,
which was true of the fixture form and not of the live one. No honest prefix
rule maps any of the four families, the refusal's remedy, so the verb could not
rename a file on this library at all, and line 10 of #178 would have refused
the same way.

**Measured cost.** Board bar (c): the naming step of the acquisition workflow
cannot run on the live library, and after the import R-407 makes the batch
unrenamable for good, so R-669's fix was unreachable in practice. Nothing
renamed wrongly.

**The fix, in the sitting.** A renamed volume or a moved mount changes a path's
prefix and never its leaf, so a dark row can be a candidate under another
spelling only when its file name is a candidate's. `_referenced` now takes the
files the pass would rename and a dark row refuses only when its leaf, keyed as
the referenced set keys a path, NFC and casefolded, is one of theirs; the
refusal lists those candidates as `could_name` beside the rows. Nothing else
about dark changed: the existence test, the exact prefix match and the
tombstone count stand, and the streamed form has a test of its own under its
live spelling. `repair paths --apply` passes its own candidates through the
same seam, and had no test over a dark row at all, so both of its reads gained
one. Driven against the live database copy: 54 candidates, 0.05 seconds, no
refusal, no staging file referenced, and a planted dark row under one
candidate's name still refuses with that file named.

**Closes when:** a dark row whose file name is a candidate's refuses and one
under another name does not, on a live row, a tombstone, a gone file under a
folder on this machine and the `/v4/catalog` form, driven through both verbs;
and `name apply --root` over download staging on the live library reaches its
gate with every acquired file planned.

**On the board bar, (c).** No issue owed: closed in the same merge.

**Closed 2026-09-23 on `unit/issue178` on its fixture condition**, sixteen
tests across `tests/test_naming_apply_cli.py` and
`tests/intake/test_repair_apply.py`, and R-523 and R-524 closed on the same
rule. The built in review at high raised six findings and four were driven in
one round: a candidate a resolved row references is never renamed, so a dark
row under its name puts nothing in doubt and the resolved keys are read before
the leaf index is built; the refusal pairs each dark row with the files it
could be naming, in row order under one cap, instead of two lists that could
not be read together; the remedy carries a second step for a row no rule can
place, R-523's own closing condition; and the cross folder leaf match and the
held candidate each have a test naming the rule. The fifth finding, the record
not yet filed, was the docs commit that followed the review's snapshot. Two
tables, `docs/mutation/r675.md` and `r675-b.md`, read in `r675-notes.md`: 23
rows, 21 killed on the subset, two zeros on existing layers the leaf rule
shadowed in every fixture, each given the test that reaches it alone and
killed on the re-run. The live condition is the sitting's, in `docs/cutover.md`
sitting 8.

**Live condition met 2026-09-23, the same sitting.** On the pipx install
rebuilt from `93e8f40`, `name apply --root` over download staging reached its
gate with 54 renames planned and nothing held, against the 582 row refusal of
the run before the fix. Record in `docs/cutover.md`, sitting 8.

`name apply`'s guard, the deletion verb refuses on this library on every run,
and no prefix rule can honestly map a streamed track.

suite behind it.

## R-677. The landing verb gates before it looks for the export, so a person answers a plan over a file that is not there

**Found:** at the eighth attended sitting, 2026-09-23. `crate intake land
--export Music/9-23-export.xml` was run before the export had been written,
and it reached its gate with the full plan, 54 files, the batch folder and
the intake file named, and the export path spelled on the screen as if it
existed. The engine checks the export before its first move, on a copy, and
would have refused `library-export-unusable` with nothing moved, so the cost
is one answer spent and one gate to re-run. The verb reads a manifest before
the gate for exactly this reason, "so a file that is not a manifest refuses
before anybody spends an answer on it", and does not do the same for the
export.

**Measured cost:** one wasted gate in the sitting, no data at risk.

**Closes when:** the landing verb asks the engine's export check before the
gate, so a missing or unusable export refuses on the plan read, with a test
that drives the plan over an absent export and reads the refusal before any
answer.

**Not on the board bar.** A shape fix; the write is still held. Issue #195,
filed after the ninth sitting for the Relay feeder.

**Closed 2026-09-23 on `relay/195`.** The engine's pre-move checks are one
function, `intake.landing.preflight`, which asks the batch name, the library,

recorded abort, apply and stale answers. Mutation tables
`docs/mutation/r677.md` and `r677-b.md`, read in `r677-notes.md`, 12

control 0 of 10128. An unreadable export was driven and refuses
`path-permission-denied` with its remedy, not an internal error, so the

## R-679. A review item outlives its question: a later resolution that owns the row leaves the version-match item open, and no verdict or predicate can retire it honestly

**Found:** at the ninth attended sitting, 2026-09-23, measured off a copy of
the queue database while deciding whether the 190 unresolved items got a
pass before line 2 of #178.

The 88 open `version-match` items were joined to job `c645`'s 206 rows by
the provider reference. **85 ask about a row that resolution now owns**, 81
under `isrc-exact` and 4 under `credited-exact`, because R-667 added the two
rules after jobs `0dbf` and `7caa` had offered them. Three are live. `offer`
is idempotent by identity, which is right, and nothing on the other side
withdraws an item when the row it asked about is settled by a rule that
never consults the queue. `crate review list` therefore says 190 questions
where 3 and the 102 label rows are real.

The verdict vocabulary is `accepted` or `rejected`. Rejecting settles the
item against every candidate and suppresses it, which is a decision the
person did not make and which would read wrong if the candidate is the very
file the ISRC rule now owns. `--where` matches `queue`, `kind` or a payload
field by equality, so `payload.why=title-approximate` would sweep 86 and
take the live Elderbrook item with them. No honest sweep exists, and a hand
pass is 85 commands recording something that did not happen.

**Measured cost:** a queue that reads as 63 times larger than it is on the
matching side, which is the shape that makes a person stop reading it. No
data at risk; the owned rows are owned and nothing downstream waits on the
stale items.

**Closes when:** a resolution that owns a row settles or withdraws that
row's open `version-match` items with a verdict that says so, distinct from
`accepted` and `rejected`, and `crate review list` on this library drops
from 190 to the three live items plus the 102 label rows, with a test that
offers an item, owns the row by ISRC on the next resolution, and reads the
item gone from the open list. A predicate that selects open items by the
row's later state is the other acceptable shape.

**Not on the board bar.** A shape fix, no write held. Issue #197, filed after
the ninth sitting for the Relay feeder.

**CLOSED in code 2026-09-23, on `relay/197`, issue #197, live measurement
owed.** A third verdict, `superseded`, written by `adjudicate` on every open
`version-match` item about a row resolution owns under `exact`, `isrc-exact`
or `credited-exact`, the actor carrying the rule; not a suppression, revocable
by `clear`, untypeable at `crate review resolve`, carried by export and import
through its own writer. Driven on a fixture under both rules and through
`match run` and the intake worker's own path. **The live count, 190 to the
three live items plus the 102 label rows, is the attended sitting's to make**:
it needs the owning job re-resolved against the live library, which a session
does not touch, so it is stated here as owed and not as done. R-680 and R-681
record what the review found at its edges.

**CLOSED live 2026-09-24, at the tenth attended sitting.** A fresh favourites
listing on the pipx install at `40daec7`, job `2026-09-24T11:49:23Z-c3ca`,
207 hearts served, resolved in 10 seconds and `crate review list --limit 500`
dropped from **190 to 105**: the three live `version-match` items, the 98
`label-release` rows and the 4 `harvested-label` rows. `--all` still lists
190, with **85 `superseded`, 81 by `isrc-exact` and 4 by `credited-exact`**,
the numbers the sitting 9 join predicted. Record in `docs/cutover.md`,
sitting 10.

## R-680. A superseded verdict outlives its rule when the row goes missing rather than back to a question

**Found:** 2026-09-23, on `relay/197`, by the built in review, then driven on
a fixture: a question retired under `isrc-exact`, the file carrying the ISRC
deleted and no other cut held, the row resolving `missing` under
`not-in-library`, and the item still reading `superseded` by `isrc-exact`.

The reopen path in `adjudicate` revokes the machine's verdict only when the
row is a question again, because that is the one state with something to
ask. A row that goes missing passes straight through, so the item keeps a
verdict asserting a rule owns a row nothing owns, until the row is either
acquired back, which makes the verdict true again, or becomes a question,
which revokes it.

**Measured cost:** `crate review list --all` reads a rule that no longer
holds, for as long as the row is missing. The open list is right, nothing
downstream reads the verdict, and acquisition fetches the row as it should.
Clearing the item on the missing path would be worse: it would put an open
question about a missing row in front of a person, with candidates that no
longer exist, which is the shape the third verdict exists to end.

**Closes when:** the record decides what a superseded item should read once
its row is missing, and whichever state is chosen is written on that path
and driven. A fourth verdict is not obviously better than a stale third.

**Not on the board bar.** A wording on a settled item, no write held.

## R-681. A list holding one line twice, with and without its ISRC, flaps the retired item with the line order

**Found:** 2026-09-23, on `relay/197`, by the built in review, then driven on
a fixture: a file carrying the row's ISRC under an artist tag the text rules
never credit, a library also holding the radio edit, and a list carrying the
line once with the ISRC, owned `isrc-exact`, and once without it, a
`version-differs` question. The two lines share one item identity, since the
identity carries no ISRC.

With the ISRC line first, the owned row retires nothing because the question
is filed after it, and the run ends with the item open. With the ISRC line
last, the question is filed and then retired, and the run ends with it
superseded. On the next run in the first order the question finds the
superseded item, revokes it and re-offers. The verdict, actor and updated
columns rewrite on every run and whether a person sees the question depends
on which line the reader emitted first.

**Measured cost:** churn on one item and an order dependent answer to "is
this a question", for a list that names the same recording twice with
different provenance. No data at risk: the row with the ISRC is owned either
way and reports so.

**Closes when:** `adjudicate` settles a row's question and its retirement
within one run by a rule that does not read the list order, for instance by
retiring after every question in the batch has been offered and letting an
owned row's retirement stand over a question the same batch asked. The cost
of that shape, a needs-review row naming an item the open list does not
show, is the one the residual titled "An offered track never becomes
listable, whatever the review answer" paid for, so the choice is the record's
and not a session's.

**Not on the board bar.** Churn on a settled item, no write held.

## R-682. The intake resolution has no by reason breakdown a renderer can read

**Found:** 2026-09-23, on `relay/196`, while building the human rendering
for R-678. The brief asked the rendering of `intake playlist --job` to name its
counts by state and by reason. The counts by state are on the `job_state`
payload's `progress`, from `intake.cli._summary`. The reason each row resolved
the way it did, `exact`, `isrc-exact`, `credited-exact`, `version-differs` and
the rest of `match.Why`, is on each item's report artifact under `why` and on
nothing the envelope carries. The renderer is a function of the envelope, and
the same brief required the json to stay byte for byte what it was, so the
breakdown cannot be rendered without adding a field the brief forbids.

**Measured cost:** a person who wants to know how many of 206 owned rows were
owned by ISRC rather than by text still reads the artifacts or `job show
--output json` for them. The counts by state, which R-678 closed on, are
printed.

**Closes when:** somebody decides whether a `by_reason` count belongs under
the intake summary's `progress`, which is a json change every consumer sees,
and if it does, `_summary` counts `why` the way it counts `state` and the
renderer prints it.

**Not on the board bar.** A missing line in a rendering, nothing false said.

**Closed 2026-09-24 on `relay/209`, issue #209.** It belongs, decided here.
`progress.by_reason` is keyed by the state word first and then by the
`match.Why` slug, `{"owned": {"exact": 190, "isrc-exact": 16}, "offered":
{...}, "missing": {...}, "suppressed": {}}`. Keyed by state because one reason
lands rows in more than one state, `title-approximate` among them, so a flat
count by reason could not say which count it explains, and keyed this way each
state's reasons sum to its own count. Every state word is a key, as every count
is; a reason is a key only when some row carries it. A report whose `why` is
absent, empty or not a string counts in its state and under no reason. The
json addition sits under `progress`, which the schema types as an open object,
so no consumer generated from it fails. `render._resolution_lines` prints each
state's reasons on the line under its count, `    by reason: exact 2`, most
rows first and ties by slug, and names a shortfall last as `unstated N` rather
than letting a partial breakdown read as complete. A progress with no
`by_reason`, from a build before this one, prints no line. Driven through
`intake playlist favorites --job` in both modes. Mutation table
`docs/mutation/r682-a`, 15 rows, every row killed.

## R-683. The drive command is found by reading the job back and comparing verb names

**Found:** 2026-09-23, on `relay/196`, by the built in review. `cli._drive_argv`
learns whether this invocation queued the job by opening the queue again after
the verb returned, reading the job, and comparing its handler's verb name with
the envelope's. The verb had the job in hand a moment earlier. The name check
is a heuristic: `intake set --job` driving an `intake.playlist` job through the
shared intake keys fails it and prints no drive, and a re-invocation that
ended with the job still queued passes it and prints the command it just ran.
The second open also pays for the queue's setup and could wait out a busy
timeout while another driver writes, only to print one line.

**Measured cost:** unmeasured on the tree. Neither misfire was driven, since
each needs a drive that ends with its job still queued, and no busy wait was
observed; a failed lookup names no drive and leaves the job line standing,
which the broad catch guarantees and `r678-b` row B3 measures.

**Closes when:** the queueing verbs record the job they enqueued on the
`Context`, as a value the envelope does not serialize, and `_emit` reads the
drive from that rather than from the queue.

**Not on the board bar.** Maintainer facing, nothing false said to a person.

## R-684. An answered landing reads and trial splices the export twice

**Found:** 2026-09-23, on `relay/195`, by the built in review. `intake land`
asks the engine's preflight on every invocation whose plan has files, before
the gate, because it cannot know whether the gate is answered until it asks.
On an answered apply the engine then asks the same preflight again under the
batch lock, so the export is read whole, copied and trial spliced twice, and
the registry read twice. Before R-677 an answered apply did it once.

**Measured cost:** unmeasured on the tree. No large export was timed. The
fixture exports are a few kilobytes, and a real collection export runs to tens
of megabytes, so the second pass is bounded by one read and one splice of that
file.

**Closes when:** the verb can tell an answered gate from an unanswered one
before it asks, through the gate rather than by reading the run record, and
skips the plan read preflight when the engine is about to ask it anyway, with
a test that counts the reads on an answered apply.

**Not on the board bar.** Efficiency only, nothing false said, nothing at
risk.

## R-685. Every verb reads the shipped taxonomy template, and the active copy on the volume is written by setup and read by doctor alone

**Found:** at the tenth attended sitting, 2026-09-24, when the plan only read
of `route inbox --export` offered 21 tracks for a `Sets and Long Tracks`
playlist that `.cratekit/coupled/taxonomy.toml` does not declare.
`taxonomy.default_taxonomy` returns the shipped template, and its docstring
says the active template "is read by the caller and passed to
`load_taxonomy` as text". No caller does. 34 call sites in 12 modules,
routing, rebuild, trees, ingest, tagging, adopt, the set builder, the label
approval and the reports, call `default_taxonomy()` and nothing in the
package loads the active file. `doctor` reads it for `taxonomy.active` and
`setup` writes it, so the declaration a person is told is theirs, and is
told to edit, changes nothing any verb does.

**Measured cost:** on this library the two differ by one section,
`[long_tracks]`, added to the shipped template by U88 on 2026-09-18, two days
after setup copied it, so the sitting's routing run built a playlist the
active declaration never asked for. Every bucket agrees, so nothing was
misfiled. The day the active file is edited, a bucket renamed or a sub added,
the edit is silent.

**Closes when:** one loader returns the library's active taxonomy from the
path `doctor` checks, falling back to the shipped template only when the
configuration names one and no active copy exists, every verb reads through
it, and a test edits the active copy and reads the change in a routing plan.
Whether a stale active copy is a doctor finding is a second decision.

**Not on the board bar.** No write held, nothing misfiled today. Issue #198, filed after the tenth sitting
for the Relay feeder.

**Closed 2026-09-24 on `relay/198`.** One loader, `core.active_taxonomy.load`,
reads the active copy at `config.state_path("taxonomy_active", cfg)`, the path
doctor's `taxonomy.active` check reads. The shipped template that
`taxonomy.template` names stands in only when the library root is a directory
and no active copy exists under it, which doctor already reports as a failure
with run setup. Every other way of not reading the copy refuses: an absent
library root as `library-volume-unmounted`, an unreadable copy and one that does
not parse as `config-unusable`, each with the remedy doctor gives. All 34 call
sites in 12 modules read through it, and the helpers with no configuration take
the declaration as a required parameter, the four tree writers whose `None`
default reached for the shipped template among them. A test walks the package's
AST, aliases resolved, and refuses the default loader, the shipped text or the
parser outside the modules allowed each. Two routing plan tests write an active
copy on the volume, one without `[long_tracks]`, this entry's measured shape,
and one renaming the long track playlist, and read each change in the plan and
the written file. The built in review's six held findings were fixed in one
round, among them `converge` opening the database before the read, which let a
refusal hold the handle. Tables `docs/mutation/r685-a.md` and `r685-b.md`,
sixteen rows, fifteen killed, the zero read in `r685-notes.md`.

**The second decision, taken conservatively: a stale active copy is not a
doctor finding.** An active copy older than the shipped template it was copied
from, and one a person edited on purpose, look the same, since nothing records
which shipped version a copy came from. A finding would tell the second person
their own declaration is wrong. R-689 records the options.

## R-686. The route.inbox.apply gate shows no plan in either output mode, so a person answers a routing plan they cannot read

**Found:** at the tenth attended sitting, 2026-09-24. `crate route inbox
--export` stopped at `route.inbox.apply` with the prompt "Apply this routing
plan to the library?", the two options and the answer command, and nothing
else: no item, no count, no digest. In json mode the gate envelope carries
`checks: []` and `summary: {}`. `run show` on the held run lists the open
gate and no plan. The only way to read the plan is to answer abort and read
the no-op envelope, then start a second run and answer apply, comparing the
two digests by hand. R-670 closed the same shape on `name.apply.confirm`,
whose gate prints every planned name.

**Measured cost:** two runs per apply, three plan only runs spent to learn
this, and a person who answers the gate as it stands approves 281 items
blind.

**Closes when:** the gate prints the plan the digest was taken over, at least
each track's destination, vocal sub, rating and long track membership with
the totals, in the default human mode, the way R-670's fix did, and the json
gate envelope carries the same items.

**Not on the board bar.** A rendering, the write is still held. Issue #199, filed after the tenth sitting
for the Relay feeder.

**Closed 2026-09-24 on `relay/199`.** `_apply_gate` passes `_shown(plan)` as the
gate's context, R-670's carry. The screen lists the digest, the count and
every item the digest was taken over, unchanged, so the json gate envelope's
`shown.items` equal the declined run's `data.items` and a test compares the
two. The export path adds its totals counted off those items: tracks, routed,
vocal, rated and long tracks, each created vocal sub by name, the dimensions
not derived, and the planner's warnings, so an intake track listed with no
destination carries its reason on the same screen. The database path of
`route inbox` shares the helper and shows its intake files (see R-691 for
what that path's plan cannot show). There is no bound, unlike R-670's
`PLAN_SHOWN`, because the digest covers every item and a list cut short asks
for approval of items nobody was shown; a first sweep over a library with
many long tracks prints one line each. An empty list in any gate's context
now renders as `none` rather than a bare header. `route unplaced` has no gate
(U91's decision), so it had nothing to render. An answered run's envelope is
unchanged. Mutation table `docs/mutation/r686.md`, twelve rows, all killed.

## R-687. A playlist imported from the rekordbox xml bridge lands at the playlist root whatever folder the file put it in, so the landing's batch playlist and the routing pass's nested subs both miss their folder and the pending steps say otherwise

**Found:** at the tenth attended sitting, 2026-09-24, twice. First on
`Music/9-23-export-3.xml`: the two batch playlists sitting 8 and 9 landed
"under INBOX" in their intake files read as direct children of the playlist
root, where rekordbox's Import Playlist put them, so `route inbox --export`
would have routed none of the 61 rows until the author dragged both into
INBOX by hand and exported again. Then on `Music/9-24-export-2.xml`, after
the author imported the 13 changed subs of `BY GENRE + ENERGY` one node at a
time, as the source system's Invariant 3 requires: each landed at the root as
a new playlist, same named ones replacing each other there, leaving three
strays, `Unsorted`, `High` and `Soul / R&B`, and every sub inside the tree
exactly as it was. The one root playlist, `Sets and Long Tracks`, landed. The
routing verb's pending text says "import the routing tree", which per the
source system's own paid for learning doubles every child of a folder that
already exists, and the landing's says "import the file", which leaves the
batch outside the folder the routing pass reads.

**Measured cost:** one rekordbox round trip at sitting 10 for the batches,
and a routing run whose 63 memberships did not land at all. The 61 rows sit
in their INBOX playlists, unrouted. Nothing lost, nothing doubled: 9998
entries and 501 playlist paths, 498 plus the three strays.

**Closes when:** the pending steps of `intake land` tell a person to drag
the imported batch playlist into the intake folder, and the pending steps of
`route inbox --export` stop naming an import that cannot land nested
membership. The membership itself lands when the tree cuts over to the
database and `route inbox` writes it without an export, which is U29's per
workflow cutover and not a wording fix. A test pins each step text.

**Not on the board bar.** The wording half is a session's, the mechanism is
attended. Issue #200, filed after the tenth sitting for the Relay feeder, scoped to the wording.

**CLOSED in wording 2026-09-24, on `relay/200`, issue #200.** `intake land`,
and `intake file` through the same `ingest.import_steps`, now has five
steps. It tells a person to import the batch playlist on its own and never
the intake folder, which would append a second copy of every batch, and to
drag the playlist from the playlist root into the intake folder, named from
the active taxonomy. `route inbox --export` names no import of the routing
tree. It says to import any root playlist the run added tracks to and nothing
else, says the nested memberships cannot land from the file, and its check
step promises only that a root playlist gains nothing on a second run.
`route unplaced --export` carried the same "import the routing tree"
sentence. Every one of its placements is nested, so its steps now name no
import at all and tell a person to file the reviewed tracks by hand. The
route-the-library skill says the same. The review drove two promises out of
the first draft: `route inbox` without `--export` reads files on disk and not
INBOX members, and `route unplaced` without `--export` only reports, so no
step may say either lands the memberships at a cutover. The inbox step also
stopped naming the ratings as something to import, since the rated tracks'
only playlists in the file are the nested batches. That leaves R-688's
decision open and removes no claim from its summary. Tests pin every step
text. The mutation table `docs/mutation/r687.md` has nine rows and all nine
were killed. Steps persisted on an intake session before this merge keep the
old text, three steps with no drag, and the refusal that replays them says
nothing false about the folder. The mechanism stays U29's. R-694 and R-695
record what the review found at the edges.

## R-688. A star rating written into an export does not land on a row rekordbox already owns

**Found:** at the tenth attended sitting, 2026-09-24. `route inbox --export`
set `Rating` on four collection rows in `9-24-export_routed.xml`, 51, 153,
204 and 255, each on a track the library already held and the author had
never rated. After the import and a fresh export, all four read `Rating="0"`.
rekordbox takes a row's attributes from the xml only for a row it creates on
that import; an owned row keeps its database values, the same rule the
source system's A2 spike found for `Location` matching. The pending text
says "import the tracks' ratings", and the proof run planned the same four
ratings again.

**Measured cost:** four ratings not set, and a pending text that promises a
result the medium cannot deliver. The screen may have shown a star on one of
the four; the author could not say, and the export is the reading recorded.

**Closes when:** the rating write moves to a medium that reaches an owned
row, the database path behind the session gates, or the export path stops
planning ratings for owned rows and its pending text stops claiming them,
with a test that pins whichever the record decides.

**Not on the board bar.** Nothing false in what was computed, the medium
cannot carry it. Issue #201, filed after the tenth sitting for the Relay feeder, scoped to the
decision and the text.

**CLOSED in code 2026-09-24, on `relay/201`, issue #201.** Decided: the export
path stops planning ratings, and it stops for every row. The brief's shape
kept a rating for rows the export creates, and that set is empty by
construction. The verb's input is a collection export taken from rekordbox,
so every row in it is one rekordbox holds. The xml rating writer only
patches a row in place and never adds one. `plan_export` in
`write/routing_cli.py` now counts, in `_owed_ratings`, the unrated rows the
source system's sort would have rated, by the same rules: a placed track, a
bucket that rates, an energy reading, and a `Rating` of empty or zero. It
returns only the count. The verb gives that count as one
`rating-not-landable` warning, on the gate's screen, on a declined run and on
an applied one. The warning says the import keeps the database's rating on
such a row and that this build writes no rating to the database. The items
lose their `rating` field, and the gate and the totals lose `rated`.
`apply_export` writes no rating. The pending summary claims none. A run
whose only change was a rating writes no file. The count joins the warnings
after the reason is decided, because no run of this medium can land it,
so counting it would answer `route-blocked` over a library already filed.
Tests in `tests/test_routing_workers.py` pin the written file's ratings
byte for byte, the count, each counting rule on a one row export, the
declined and gate warnings, and `nothing-to-route` on a re-run that still
owes ratings. The mutation table `docs/mutation/r688.md` has fifteen rows and
all fifteen were killed. The rating itself lands only when a database path
writes it. `write/metadata.plan_rating_backfill` is a FILL IF EMPTY planner
for that write and has no caller, so this is the cutover's. R-696 and R-697
record what this decision left at its edges.

## R-689. Nothing records which shipped template an active copy was made from, so a copy that fell behind the shipped template cannot be told from one a person edited

**Found:** on `relay/198`, 2026-09-24, deciding R-685's second question.
Setup copies the shipped template beside the database and records only its
short name, `taxonomy.template`. The shipped template then gains sections, as
`[long_tracks]` arrived with U88 two days after the tenth sitting's library was
set up. Since R-685 every verb reads the active copy, so a section the shipped
template gained after setup is now absent from every verb, where before it was
present in every verb whatever the active copy said.

**Measured cost:** on the tenth sitting's library, the long track playlist
stops being planned, which is what that library's declaration asks for. No
other difference was measured. A person who wants a section added upstream has
no way to learn it arrived.

**Closes when:** the record decides between three options and a test pins the
choice. Setup records a digest of the shipped text it copied, and doctor
reports INFO when the shipped template has moved on and the active copy still
matches the recorded digest, which is a copy nobody edited. Or doctor reports a
per section difference as INFO whatever the history. Or nothing, stated in
doctor's OK detail. The branch that filed this took the third, by not adding a
finding.

**Not on the board bar.** Maintainer facing, nothing false is said and no
write is held.

**Closed 2026-09-24 on `relay/205`, issue #205.** The first option. Setup
writes `taxonomy.origin.toml` beside the copy, the template's short name and
a sha256 of the shipped text it copied, a COUPLED state file so a restore
rolls it back with the copy it describes, and only for a copy it makes:
setup cannot know which text a copy it left alone came from, and a record
written anyway would say "unedited" over a copy nothing established that
about. Doctor's `taxonomy.active` compares three digests, the recorded one,
the copy's and the shipped text's as it ships now, by a `Fingerprint` that
`core/taxonomy` computes so doctor never holds the shipped text beside the
parser. A copy that still matches the record while the shipped text moved on
is INFO, naming the top level sections the shipped template gained and the
ones it dropped, or "inside sections both declare" when neither. A copy that
differs from the record is OK as edited, and what the shipped text did since
is not raised. No record, which is every library set up before this, is OK
with the origin said to be unrecorded and whether the copy matches the shipped
text now; a record that cannot be read or used, or that names a template
other than the configured one, is INFO with the reason. Doctor never writes
the copy. The second option was not taken because it would flag every
deliberate edit for life, and the third because the live library's case would
stay unexplained. The tenth sitting's shape is pinned in
`tests/test_doctor.py`, an older copy under a record of that older text.
Fourteen tests. The mutation table is authored, twelve rows, and NOT
measured, `docs/mutation/r689-notes.md` says why. R-707 records that a copy
made before this has no way to gain a record.

## R-690. A job re-reads the active taxonomy per item and on resume, so an edit made while a job is open changes the declaration its remaining items are judged by

**Found:** by the built in review on `relay/198`, 2026-09-24, four findings of
one shape. The tag, retag, census and adoption workers each call
`active_taxonomy.load(cfg)` per item, `handle_resort` reads it again for its
left behind report after the engine read it, and the database routing verb
reads it once for its plan and again in `apply_inbox` after the gate. The plan
digests cover the items, not the declaration, so an edit between the plan and
the last item is not refused as stale. The vocal threshold is read the same
way and is documented as read as it stands (U89), so this is that precedent
applied to the taxonomy, not a new rule.

**Measured cost:** not driven. It needs a person to edit the active copy while
a job is open or between an interrupted job and its resume. Before R-685 an
edit changed nothing at all, so no run on main could reach it. The per item read
costs one small file read and parse per item on the library volume, where it
used to parse packaged data per item.

**Closes when:** a job freezes the declaration it was planned against, as a
digest in the payload that a resume compares and refuses on as
`decision-stale`, or as the text itself, and the export and database routing
verbs pass one read from plan to write, with a test that edits the active copy
between a plan and its apply and reads the refusal.

**Not on the board bar.** Reachability unmeasured, and the precedent it
follows is documented.

**Narrowed 2026-09-24, on `relay/202` (R-691).** The database routing verb
now reads the declaration once, in `route_inbox`, and carries it on the plan
to `apply_inbox`, so the second read after the gate is gone for that verb.
The per item reads in the workers and the resort's second read stand, and
no digest covers the declaration yet.

## R-691. The database route inbox gate shows the intake files and no destination, because that path's plan is the file list and the routing is decided after the answer

**Found:** by the built in review on `relay/199`, 2026-09-24, while R-686 was
closed. `route inbox` without `--export` builds its plan from `_inbox_items`,
each file's path and name, and decides where each goes inside `apply_inbox`
after the gate. R-686's fix shows that plan, so the gate now lists the files,
but not one destination, and the digest binds the file list and not where
the files go.

**Measured cost:** not driven on a library; the path needs a tree that has
cut over, and the tenth sitting ran the export medium. A person answering it
approves a routing whose destinations they have not seen.

**Closes when:** the database path plans its placements before the gate, the
items carry each file's destination the way the export items do, and the
digest is taken over them, with a test reading a destination off the gate's
`shown`.

**Not on the board bar.** The write is still held behind the gate, and the
path is reached only once a tree has cut over.

**Closed 2026-09-24 on `relay/202`, issue #202.** `plan_inbox` in
`write/routing_cli.py` decides every placement before the gate, by the calls
the write made after it: `read_truth` per file, `declared_membership`
through the registry's source for each tree that has cut over, once per
source, and `routing_pass.destination` for the display names, the export
path's own naming. Each item carries `path`, `name`, `destination` and
`vocal`, the digest is taken over them, and a reading that moves a
placement moves the digest over one unchanged folder. The gate's facts are
counted off the items as the export gate's are: the intake folder, tracks,
routed, vocal, the trees the write goes into, the dimensions not derived
and the planner's warnings. `apply_inbox` consumes the plan it is handed,
the placements, the declaration and the registry, and derives nothing a
second time, so the row lands under the folder and playlist the screen
named and the declaration is read once per verb, which narrows R-690 for
this verb. A library with nothing native reads no file and no calibration,
lists its files with no destination, and carries the export remedy on the
gate and on the declined and empty answers alike; the apply still answers
`no-native-tree`. What the path writes is unchanged. The review drove the
calibration read back under the native check, since the first draft refused
a library that could not use the cut, and put the planner's warnings on
every answer. Mutation table `docs/mutation/r691.md`, sixteen rows, all
killed. The route-the-library skill says the gate shows the plan. R-698
records what moving the derivation before the gate left at its edge.

## R-692. The route gate names each track by its export id and its rating on the raw byte scale, so a person reads numbers rather than songs and stars

**Found:** by the built in review on `relay/199`, 2026-09-24. The gate R-686
opened lists the plan's items as they are, so a line reads
`track_id=11, destination=Deep House/Low, ..., rating=255`. The id is the
export's TrackID, and 255 is five stars on rekordbox's 0 to 255 scale. The
export row the planner already read carries the artist and the title.

**Measured cost:** a person has to look each id up in the export to know
which song a line files, and has to know the byte scale to read the rating.
Not driven at a sitting.
